General
considerations
■
■Usually smoked in
cigarettes (induces
CYP1A2)
■

and CYP2D68,9

respiratory depression

■

■
■Arrhythmia possible
■

cocaine – may be fatal
■
■MDMA (3,4-methylenedioxymetham-

ecstasy10
■
■Sedative
■

possible
■

enzymes
■

causes uncon-
sciousness
■
■Onset of effects
may be rapid
if snorted or
injected
Older
antipsychotics
■
■Antipsychotics reduce the psychotropic effects of almost all drugs of abuse by blocking dopamine receptors (dopamine is the neu-
rotransmitter responsible for ‘reward’, e.g. haloperidol and MDMA11)
■
■Patients prescribed antipsychotics may increase their consumption of illicit substances to compensate
■
■Patients who have taken ecstasy may be more prone to EPS
■
■Cardiotoxic or very sedative antipsychotics are best avoided, at least initially. Sulpiride is a reasonably safe first choice
■
■Methamphetamines increase the risk of EPS with haloperidol12
Second-
generation
antipsychotics
■
■Risk of additive seda-
tion
■

tobacco can reduce
plasma levels of olan-
zapine and clozapine
via induction of
CYP1A213
■
■Clozapine might
reduce cannabis and
alcohol consumption14
■
■Outcome of THC/CBD
inhibition of CYP1A2
unknown
■
■Risk of additive sedation
■

withdrawal being precipitated

■

increasing methadone levels,
especially in those with slowed

■

cocaine-induced euphoria17–21
■
■Olanzapine may worsen cocaine
dependency22
■
